claims.source: Given that isolated SAM domains are sufficient to undergo polymerization in vitro (Kim et al., 2001; Qiao et al., 2004), it is likely that SAM-mediated self-association of Yan occurs both on and off DNA, and that competition for Yan molecules between the two pools could be a key feature that shapes Yan DNA occupancy, and ultimately repression.
claims.evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the modeling and experimental results.

claims.claim: Smaller-order Yan species can diffuse effectively in order to bind their targets on DNA.
claims.source: A key assumption of the approach is that smaller-order Yan species can diffuse effectively in order to bind their targets on DNA, but as Yan oligomers increase in size, the inverse relationship between particle size and diffusion rate, as described by the Stokes–Einstein relation (Berg and von Hippel, 1985), will eventually prevent diffusion and DNA binding.
claims.evidence: This is an assumption based on physical principles and cited literature.

claims.claim: As Yan oligomers increase in size, the inverse relationship between particle size and diffusion rate will eventually prevent diffusion and DNA binding.
claims.source: A key assumption of the approach is that smaller-order Yan species can diffuse effectively in order to bind their targets on DNA, but as Yan oligomers increase in size, the inverse relationship between particle size and diffusion rate, as described by the Stokes–Einstein relation (Berg and von Hippel, 1985), will eventually prevent diffusion and DNA binding.
claims.evidence: This is based on the Stokes-Einstein relation and cited literature.

claims.claim: Differences in bulk diffusion rates have been observed in vivo for Yan wildtype, monomers, and dimers.
claims.source: Although there have been no direct measurements of Yan diffusion rates on a precise polymer-species basis, differences in bulk diffusion rates have been observed in vivo for Yan wildtype, monomers, and dimers (Zhang et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: At wildtype Yan SAM affinity, fractional occupancy at ETS sites was predicted to be almost the same at lower concentrations of Yan, regardless of off-DNA polymerization.
claims.source: In the case of wildtype Yan SAM affinity (Figure 1A), fractional occupancy at ETS sites was predicted to be almost the same at lower concentrations of Yan, regardless of off-DNA polymerization.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: At higher concentrations of Yan, the calculation that included polymerization off of DNA predicted a drop in occupancy.
claims.source: However, at higher concentrations of Yan, the calculation that included polymerization off of DNA predicted a drop in occupancy (Figure 1A, black solid curve), whereas that in which only on-DNA polymerization was permitted predicted sustained high occupancy (Figure 1A, grey dashed curve).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Low values of self-association affinity (0 to −5 kcal/mol) produced occupancy only at the high end of the physiological Yan concentration range.
claims.source: For example, low values of self-association affinity (0 to −5 kcal/mol) produced occupancy only at the high end of the physiological Yan concentration range, whereas increased self-association strength (−10 to −14 kcal/mol) permitted occupancy only at sub-physiological Yan concentrations (Figure 1D, blue shading).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Increased self-association strength (−10 to −14 kcal/mol) permitted occupancy only at sub-physiological Yan concentrations.
claims.source: For example, low values of self-association affinity (0 to −5 kcal/mol) produced occupancy only at the high end of the physiological Yan concentration range, whereas increased self-association strength (−10 to −14 kcal/mol) permitted occupancy only at sub-physiological Yan concentrations (Figure 1D, blue shading).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the modeling results shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The incorporation of off-DNA polymerization suggests that saturated DNA binding will only occur under regimes of moderate self-association where adequate pools of lower-order Yan species remain available to bind DNA.
claims.source: Thus in contrast to the previous model's prediction that increasing Yan concentration will drive saturated DNA binding across the SAM–SAM affinity range (Hope et al., 2017), the incorporation of off-DNA polymerization suggests this will only occur under regimes of moderate self-association where adequate pools of lower-order Yan species remain available to bind DNA.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results comparing on-DNA only versus on- and off-DNA polymerization.

claims.claim: Yan monomers show genome-wide chromatin occupancy patterns that are similar to those of wildtype polymerization-competent Yan.
claims.source: Providing further validation to our assumption, prior work has found that Yan monomers show genome-wide chromatin occupancy patterns that are similar to those of wildtype polymerization-competent Yan (Webber et al., 2013), although repressive function is compromised.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published ChIP-seq data.

claims.claim: Monomerizing mutations in the SAM domain do not alter Yan's DNA binding ability in vitro.
claims.source: In addition, in vitro studies have shown that monomerizing mutations in the SAM domain, which is outside of the DNA-binding ETS domain, do not alter Yan's DNA binding ability (Qiao et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published in vitro binding studies.

claims.claim: Three orders of magnitude difference has been measured for the Yan SAM–SAM interaction versus that of its human counterpart TEL.
claims.source: To engineer Yan mutants with increased affinity, we capitalized on the three orders of magnitude difference that has been measured for the Yan SAM–SAM interaction versus that of its human counterpart TEL (Kim et al., 2001; Qiao et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published affinity measurements.

claims.claim: Of the 22 residues at the SAM–SAM interface in the TEL crystal structure, nine were divergent between TEL and Yan.
claims.source: We reasoned that of the 22 residues at the SAM–SAM interface in the TEL crystal structure, the nine that were divergent between TEL and Yan were probably responsible for this affinity difference (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis of the TEL crystal structure and sequence alignment.

claims.claim: Four of the nine divergent residues clustered in a small region at the periphery of the SAM–SAM interface.
claims.source: Four of the nine clustered in a small region at the periphery of the SAM–SAM interface, and three of these made salt-bridge contacts that span that interface.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Three of the four clustered divergent residues made salt-bridge contacts that span the SAM–SAM interface.
claims.source: Four of the nine clustered in a small region at the periphery of the SAM–SAM interface, and three of these made salt-bridge contacts that span that interface.
claims.evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Mutating a subset of the four clustered residues had previously been shown to decrease TEL's polymerization affinity in vitro and to block the transformation ability of TEL oncogenic fusions in cultured cells.
claims.source: Mutating a subset of these residues had previously been shown to decrease TEL's polymerization affinity in vitro and to block the transformation ability of TEL oncogenic fusions in cultured cells (Cetinbas et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to published research.

claims.claim: The wild type Yan SAM domain ran primarily as monomers and dimers, with some high-order species, consistent with its low μM affinity.
claims.source: The wild type Yan SAM domain ran primarily as monomers and dimers, with some high-order species, consistent with its low μM affinity (Figure 2C; Qiao et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the native gel assay results shown in Figure 2C and cited affinity measurements.

claims.claim: The negGFP native gel assay identified Yan SAM variants that matched and exceeded the polymerization strength of TEL SAM.
claims.source: The mobility shifts observed in the negGFP native gel assay identified Yan SAM variants that matched and exceeded the polymerization strength of TEL SAM (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the native gel assay results shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: YT15 (SY5) surpassed the extent of polymerization by TEL SAM.
claims.source: Although two individual mutants, R92K and G96R, modulated mobility on their own (YT7 and YT8, respectively), multiple mutations were required for greater shifts, with simultaneous mutation of all four residues (YT15) surpassing the extent of polymerization by TEL SAM.
claims.evidence: This is supported by the native gel assay results shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Four orders of magnitude separate the binding affinities of wildtype Yan and SY5.
claims.source: The Kds measured by SPR followed the rank order predicted by the native gel shift assay and revealed that four orders of magnitude separate the binding affinities of wildtype Yan and SY5 (Figure 3A–C and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the SPR measurements shown in Figure 3.

claims.claim: The calculated wildtype Yan affinity of 5.6 uM closely matched the previously measured value of 7 uM.
claims.source: Our calculation of the wildtype Yan affinity as 5.6 uM closely matched the previously measured value of 7 uM (Qiao et al., 2004), validating the quality of our fusion proteins.
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of the SPR measurement to published data.

claims.claim: The measurements of 6.7 nM for SY4 and 0.13 nM for SY5 coincide with their migration relative to TEL (2 nM) on the native gels.
claims.source: In addition, our measurements of 6.7 nM for SY4 and 0.13 nM for SY5 coincide with their migration relative to TEL (2 nM, Kim et al., 2001) on the native gels (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of SPR measurements to native gel mobility and cited TEL affinity.

claims.claim: There is non-linearity between mobility on the native gel and affinity.
claims.source: We also noted non-linearity between mobility on the native gel and affinity, as the rather modest mobility shift of SY1 (YT8) relative to that of the wildtype Yan SAM coincided with a two orders of magnitude decrease in Kd.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from comparing native gel mobility to SPR-measured affinities.

claims.claim: SY1–5 showed increasingly robust co-immunoprecipation under stringent conditions in which the wildtype Yan–Yan interaction was not detectable.
claims.source: Under stringent conditions in which the wildtype Yan–Yan interaction was not detectable, SY1–5 showed increasingly robust co-immunoprecipation (Figure 3D), which was roughly proportional with their measured affinities (Figure 2C).

claims.claim: Robust interactions were observed in both directions between Yan wildtype and SY5 in pair-wise co-immunoprecipitations.

We observed robust interactions in both directions (Figure 3—figure supplement 3, lanes 6 and 7).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the co-IP results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: All three yanSY homozygotes (yanSY3, yanSY4, yanSY5) were viable, in contrast to yan null homozygotes which die as embryos.
claims.source: In contrast to yan null homozygotes, 100% of which die as embryos (Webber et al., 2013), all three yanSY homozygotes were viable.

claims.claim: The viability of the yanSY5 allele in trans to a yan null allele showed strong lethality compared to wildtype.
claims.source: The viability of the yanSY5 allele in trans to a yan null allele also showed strong lethality compared to wildtype (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by the viability data shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Embryonic lethality increased from 8% in the wildtype control to approximately 25% in yanSY3, 30% in yanSY4, and 40% in yanSY5.
claims.source: Lethality increased from 8% in the wildtype control to approximately 25% in yanSY3, 30% in yanSY4, and 40% in yanSY5 (Figure 4B), suggesting that the reduced viability (Figure 4A) results primarily, but not entirely, from embryonic lethality.

claims.source: Focusing on yanSY4 and yanSY5, defects in the anterior portion of the head cuticle were noted in the dead embryos, consistent with the classic yan 'anterior-open' loss-of-function phenotype (Nusslein-Volhard et al., 1984; Rogge et al., 1995).

claims.claim: SuperYan animals that survived to adulthood eclosed with rough eyes.
claims.source: Finally, as discussed further below, SuperYan animals that survived to adulthood eclosed with rough eyes, consistent with Yan's known roles in eye development (Lai and Rubin, 1992).

claims.claim: SY5 showed a reduced ability to repress transcription compared to wildtype Yan in transfected cultured cells.

claims.claim: Subcellular distribution and signaling responsiveness of SY5 were indistinguishable from those of the wildtype.

claims.claim: Overall Yan levels appeared increased in the SuperYan mutants compared to wildtype.

results.result: Mathematical modeling predicts that off-DNA polymerization creates a regime where strong SAM-SAM interactions sequester Yan away from DNA. At wildtype affinity, off-DNA polymerization reduces occupancy only at high Yan concentrations. Across a range of affinities, saturated DNA binding occurs only under moderate self-association where lower-order species remain available.
results.evaluation: Claims C29, C43-C44, C47-C49 collectively describe modeling predictions that are internally consistent and supported by the computational results shown in Figure 1. The model incorporates biophysical principles (Stokes-Einstein relation) and produces testable predictions about the relationship between SAM affinity and DNA occupancy.

results.result: A structure-guided mutagenesis screen identified four residues at the Yan SAM-SAM interface whose substitution increased binding affinity over four orders of magnitude (5.6 μM to 0.13 nM). Native gel assays and SPR measurements confirmed a graded series of SuperYan (SY1-5) mutants spanning this affinity range.
results.evaluation: Claims C30, C52-C63 describe a systematic mutagenesis approach with multiple orthogonal validation methods (native gels, SPR, co-IP). The measured affinities are internally consistent across assays, and the wildtype measurement (5.6 μM) matches published values (7 μM), validating the approach. The structural rationale based on TEL-Yan divergence is sound.

results.result: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrated that SY1-5 mutants show increasingly robust self-association under stringent conditions, and that wildtype Yan and SY5 can form heterotypic complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 are supported by the co-IP data in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 3. The graded increase in co-IP signal correlates with measured affinities, and the bidirectional heterotypic interactions are clearly demonstrated. However, the interpretation that stronger co-IP in one direction (lane 6 vs 7) reflects homotypic SY5-SY5 interactions is speculative.

results.result: CRISPR-generated yanSY3-5 alleles are viable but show reduced fitness and increased embryonic lethality that correlates with SAM affinity. YanSY5 shows the strongest phenotypes including ~40% embryonic lethality with anterior-open defects and rough adult eyes.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C71 are well-supported by the viability data (Figure 4A-B) and phenotypic observations. The graded severity correlating with affinity strengthens the conclusion. Statistical tests (chi-square) are appropriate. The comparison to yan null lethality provides important context. The anterior-open phenotype is consistent with known yan loss-of-function.

results.result: Overexpression experiments and transcription assays demonstrate that SuperYan mutants have reduced repressive activity compared to wildtype Yan. SY5 shows significantly impaired transcriptional repression while maintaining normal subcellular localization and signaling responsiveness.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76 are supported by overexpression phenotypes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and transcription assays (Figure 4C). The inverse correlation between SAM affinity and phenotypic severity is striking. The comparable protein levels and localization (C74, C76) rule out trivial explanations. However, only SY5 shows statistically significant reduction in the transcription assay (C75), while SY3-4 are indistinguishable from wildtype.

results.result: SuperYan mutants show dramatically increased formation of punctate structures throughout eye imaginal discs (10-20 fold increase) and ~50% elevated total Yan levels. This cellular phenotype matches modeling predictions of off-DNA sequestration.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are strongly supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 5). The quantification is rigorous (n=6 measurements, appropriate statistics). The 10-20 fold increase in puncta is dramatic and correlates with SAM affinity. The connection to modeling predictions (C81) is reasonable but somewhat inferential—puncta could reflect other aggregation mechanisms.

results.result: Genetic manipulations that reduce effective polymerization—heterozygosity with wildtype Yan or overexpression of hyperactive MAPK—dramatically reduce SY5 puncta formation, supporting a sequestration model where increased polymerization drives aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C87 are supported by the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1. Both manipulations produce the predicted effects. The interpretation that wildtype Yan intercalates into SY polymers (C85) is reasonable given the co-IP data, though direct evidence for 'capping' is lacking. The MAPK result (C86) is particularly compelling as it connects to known Yan regulation.

results.result: SuperYan mutants show photoreceptor over-recruitment with a striking bias: ~30% of ommatidia have extra outer (R3/R4) photoreceptors while <10% have extra R7s. This pattern differs markedly from other yan hypomorphs and is confirmed by increased Salm expression in larval discs.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 are well-supported by histological sections (Figure 6G-I), quantification (Figure 6F), and marker analysis (Figure 6L, O). The differential effect on R3/R4 vs R7 is striking and statistically robust. The Salm and Pros staining in larval discs corroborates the adult phenotypes. This is a novel observation that distinguishes SuperYan from other yan alleles.

results.result: Comparison to published yan alleles reveals that SuperYan mutants have an inverted phenotypic ratio compared to yan1 and yanP: strong R3/R4 but weak R7 phenotypes. This suggests that SY can assemble functional complexes for R7 regulation but not for R3/R4 regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C98 make a compelling comparison to published data. The cited frequencies for yan1 (88% extra R7s, 27% extra outers) and yanP (20% extra R7s, rare outers) provide clear context. The interpretation (C98) that SY retains function for R7 but not R3/R4 is reasonable given the data, though it remains somewhat inferential.

results.result: The monomeric yanV105R allele shows the opposite pattern from SuperYan: strong R7 phenotype (70% extra R7s) with moderate R3/R4 phenotype (28% extra outers), confirmed in both adult sections and larval disc marker expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 are supported by histological data (Figure 6F, J) and marker analysis (Figure 6M, P). The phenotype is consistent with published characterization of yanV105R as a strong hypomorph. This provides a critical comparison point for interpreting the SuperYan phenotypes and supports the model of differential oligomer requirements.

results.result: ChIP-seq analysis identified a high-confidence Yan binding peak upstream of salm in eye discs but not in embryos, suggesting context-specific regulation. No significant occupancy was detected at the known pros enhancer, while aos and aop showed similar occupancy in both tissues.
results.evaluation: Claims C102-C106 are supported by ChIP-seq data (Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1) with MACS peak calling. The context-specific occupancy at salm is interesting and well-documented. However, the failure to detect pros occupancy (C105) is concerning given pros is a known Yan target. The authors acknowledge this limitation and offer reasonable speculation (C111), but it raises questions about ChIP sensitivity.

results.result: ChIP-qPCR validation shows that SY5 occupancy at salm is less than half that of wildtype Yan, while occupancy at aos and aop is equivalent. This suggests that salm regulation is uniquely sensitive to Yan polymerization state.
results.evaluation: Claims C107-C113 are supported by ChIP-qPCR data (Figure 7E) with appropriate replication (n=3) and statistics. The differential effect on salm vs aos/aop is clear and statistically significant. This is a key result connecting altered polymerization to target-specific effects. However, the sample size is modest and only one R3/R4-specific target is examined.

results.result: A salm reporter is repressed by wildtype Yan but shows reduced repression by SY5 in transcription assays. In vivo, the salm reporter shows R3/R4-specific de-repression in yanSY5 discs but not wildtype, while a pros reporter is unaffected.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C118 are supported by transcription assays (Figure 7F) and reporter expression in discs (Figure 7G-J). The cell-type-specific de-repression of the salm reporter in yanSY5 background is compelling. The pros reporter control strengthens the conclusion. However, the salm reporter shows weaker induction than the king tubby reporter, raising questions about its sensitivity.

results.result: Salm is identified as a novel direct R3/R4-specific target of Yan whose regulation is uniquely sensitive to increased Yan polymerization.
results.evaluation: Claims C119-C120 synthesize multiple lines of evidence: ChIP-seq peak, ChIP-qPCR validation, reduced SY5 occupancy, transcription assays, and in vivo reporter de-repression. The convergence of these results strongly supports salm as a direct Yan target. The R3/R4 specificity is well-demonstrated. The claim of unique sensitivity to polymerization is supported but based on limited comparison (mainly aos and aop).

results.result: The authors propose a model where increased SAM affinity drives off-DNA sequestration, limiting functional complex formation. Different Yan polymer distributions regulate different target genes, and tuning SAM affinity to a middle regime optimizes these requirements.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C123 represent the central model integrating all results. The sequestration model (C121) is well-supported by modeling, puncta formation, and functional defects. The proposal of differential polymer requirements (C122-C123) is supported by the contrasting phenotypes of SuperYan vs monomeric Yan and the differential target sensitivity. However, direct evidence for specific polymer sizes at specific targets is lacking.

results.result: The authors conclude that protein-protein interaction affinity must be evolutionarily tuned to balance complex stability with assembly capability. This principle likely extends beyond polymerizing TFs to many transcription factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C128 represent broader conclusions and principles derived from the Yan results. The core principle (C124) is well-supported by the experimental data showing loss-of-function from both too-weak and too-strong interactions. The extension to other TFs (C126-C127) is reasonable speculation supported by general principles, though direct evidence is limited to Yan.

results.result: The authors propose that target genes requiring lower-order Yan species (like salm/R3/R4 genes) are most compromised by increased SAM affinity, while those requiring higher-order species (like R7 genes) are most sensitive to reduced affinity. This explains the differential phenotypes of SuperYan vs monomeric Yan.
results.evaluation: Claims C133-C139 present a mechanistic model to explain the differential phenotypes. The model is logical and consistent with the data, but it remains largely speculative. Direct evidence for the oligomeric state of Yan at specific targets is lacking. The model makes testable predictions but requires additional experiments (e.g., measuring Yan oligomer distributions in vivo, testing intermediate affinity mutants on specific targets).

results.result: The modeling assumes that smaller Yan species can diffuse effectively to bind DNA, while larger oligomers have reduced diffusion. This is supported by the Stokes-Einstein relation, published observations of differential diffusion rates for Yan wildtype/monomers/dimers, and ChIP-seq data showing similar occupancy patterns for monomers and wildtype.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C42, C50-C51 describe key modeling assumptions that are reasonably justified. The Stokes-Einstein relation is well-established physics. The cited diffusion differences (C42) and ChIP-seq similarity (C50) provide experimental support. However, the assumption that only monomers nucleate DNA binding is simplifying—the control calculations allowing dimers and trimers (mentioned in text) would strengthen this.

results.result: The comparable ratio of total to nuclear Yan in wildtype and SuperYan discs suggests that cytoplasmic self-association primarily slows degradation rather than affecting nuclear import.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 present an interpretation of the comparable total:nuclear ratios. While the observation (C82) is supported by the data in Figure 5, the mechanistic interpretation (C83) is speculative. Alternative explanations (e.g., compensatory changes in import/export rates) are not ruled out. This would require direct measurements of protein stability and import/export kinetics.

results.result: Recent imaging studies show that eukaryotic TFs rely on 3D diffusion with transient chromatin associations. Strong SAM affinity should increase time in higher-order complexes, limiting diffusion-based search. Conversely, monomeric Yan may have insufficient residence time to form stable complexes despite effective diffusion.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C130 accurately cite published imaging studies. Claims C131-C132 are reasonable inferences connecting these principles to the Yan results. However, C132 is speculative—no direct measurements of Yan residence times are presented. The logic is sound but would benefit from experimental validation (e.g., single-molecule tracking).

results.result: The authors propose two non-exclusive mechanisms for context-specific regulation: (1) regulatory grammar where different binding site arrangements favor different oligomer sizes, and (2) signaling-mediated modulation of polymerization. They speculate that heterotypic vs homotypic sites could facilitate smaller vs larger complexes, and that AP-1 factors might mediate heterotypic Yan complexes.
results.evaluation: Claims C141-C145 present speculative mechanisms that are logical but lack direct experimental support. The importance of tandem ETS sites (C144) is documented, but the specific predictions about heterotypic vs homotypic sites (C143) are untested. The speculation about AP-1 factors (C145) is based on genetic interactions and mammalian data but needs direct testing in the Yan system.

results.result: The authors propose that differential RTK signaling levels could modulate Yan polymerization in different cell types. High RTK signaling in R7 precursors might disrupt SY polymers more effectively than lower signaling in R3/R4 cells. This is supported by the observation that MAPK overexpression reduces SY5 puncta and the proximity of a key MAPK phosphorylation site to the SAM domain.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C150 present a plausible mechanism connecting signaling levels to polymerization. The rlSEM overexpression result (C148) supports the general idea that MAPK can modulate polymerization. However, the specific proposal about differential effects in R7 vs R3/R4 (C147) is speculative and not directly tested. The proximity of the phosphorylation site (C149) is suggestive but the mechanistic speculation (C150) requires experimental validation.

results.result: The authors speculate that Yan may use smaller species for accurate recognition of single enhancer sites (like salm) and larger polymers for coordinated repression across loci with broader occupancy (like aos/aop). This is consistent with prior ChIP-seq data showing reduced peak density at extensively occupied loci in Yan monomers.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C154 present an interesting model connecting oligomer size to regulatory mode. The speculation is logical and consistent with the differential ChIP occupancy patterns. The reference to prior monomer ChIP-seq data (C155) provides some support. However, this remains largely speculative without direct measurements of oligomer distributions at specific loci or functional tests of the model.

results.result: The authors discuss how TEL might function with nanomolar affinity, proposing several possibilities: lower expression levels, heterotypic interactions, post-translational modifications, or that extensive off-DNA polymerization provides a regulatory strategy. They note that SY5 has even stronger affinity than TEL, suggesting TEL is tuned to sub-maximal affinity.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C160 present reasonable speculation about TEL function. The observation that SY5 is stronger than TEL (C159-C160) is well-supported by the data. However, the various explanations for how TEL operates (C156-C158) are entirely speculative without measurements of TEL expression levels, interaction partners, or modifications in relevant contexts. These are interesting hypotheses for future work.

results.result: The mutagenesis results emphasize the importance of charged residues at the SAM interface periphery. SY5 represents the strongest quantitatively measured SAM-SAM interaction, suggesting evolutionary selection against sub-nanomolar affinities to prevent excessive aggregation.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C162 are well-supported by the structural analysis and mutagenesis results, with validation from prior TEL studies. Claim C163 is supported by comparison to published SAM affinity measurements. Claim C164 is a reasonable inference but somewhat speculative—the evolutionary argument assumes SY5-like affinities would be deleterious across contexts, which is supported by the Yan data but not directly tested in other SAM-containing proteins.

results.result: The authors speculate that Yan puncta may represent phase-separated complexes. They note that wildtype Yan shows some puncta, that low-complexity domains important for phase separation are enriched in TFs including Yan, and that Yan's genome-wide occupancy patterns resemble super-enhancers.
results.evaluation: Claims C165-C166 accurately cite the phase separation literature. Claims C167-C169 present interesting speculation connecting Yan puncta to phase separation. The observations (some wildtype puncta, presence of disordered regions, super-enhancer-like patterns) are consistent with phase separation but not definitive. Direct tests of phase separation behavior (e.g., FRAP, sensitivity to 1,6-hexanediol, in vitro droplet formation) are needed.
